messages.subject: optimizing hierarchical non-linear regression
parts:
Hi all, I'm running a hierarchical non-linear regression with 3D multinormal random effects. I adapted the code from section 5.12 of the STAN manual for this task, hoping to maintain as much speed as possible since the data set has 70K individuals and 450K observations. It's working but, as expected, pretty slow in that it takes ~5 minutes per HMC iteration (it still converges in a reasonable # of iterations). I'm wondering if there are any other obvious tricks to speed things up here. For instance, I get the feeling that the for (n in 1:Nobs) loop could be vectorized to be faster but am not sure whether that's true or, if so, how. Any help is much appreciated!!

Thanks,

Steve

data {
  int<lower=0> Nobs; // # observations
  int<lower=1> Npat; // # individuals
  int<lower=1> NcovsPat; // # individual-level predictors (1, sex)
  int<lower=1> NasymParm; // # parameters for non-linear model
  int<lower=1,upper=Npat> jj[Nobs]; // individual for observation
  vector[Nobs] time;    // time of follow up
  matrix[Npat,NcovsPat] Upat;    // individual-level predictors [1, sex]_jj
  vector[Nobs] y;    // outcome
}
parameters {
  matrix[NasymParm,Npat] z;
  cholesky_factor_corr[NasymParm] CovsPatOmega; // correlation matrix for predictor-coefficients
  vector<lower=0>[NasymParm] tau; // prior scale on covar-var matrix
  matrix[NcovsPat,NasymParm] gamma; // individual-level coefficients (1,sex)X(Asym,R0,lrc)
  real<lower=0> sigma; // obs-level error
}
transformed parameters {
  matrix[Npat,NasymParm] beta; // individual-level predictors, each row is a NasymParm-length vector
  vector[Npat] Asym;      // Asymptote
  vector[Npat] R0;      // Initial value
  vector[Npat] lrc;      // log rate of change
  matrix[NasymParm,NasymParm] Sigma_beta; // reparameterize as cov-var matrix
  beta <- Upat * gamma + (diag_pre_multiply(tau,CovsPatOmega) * z)';
  Asym <- col(beta,1);
  R0 <- col(beta,2);
  lrc <- col(beta,3);
  Sigma_beta <- diag_pre_multiply(tau,CovsPatOmega) * diag_pre_multiply(tau,CovsPatOmega)'; // Recalculate as covar-var matrix
}
model {
  vector[Nobs] Mod_jj;
  for (n in 1:Nobs) {
    Mod_jj[n] <- Asym[jj[n]] + (R0[jj[n]] - Asym[jj[n]]) * exp(-exp(lrc[jj[n]]) * time[n]);
  }
  y ~ normal(Mod_jj, sigma);
  tau ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
  to_vector(z) ~ normal(0,1);
  CovsPatOmega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2);
  to_vector(gamma) ~ normal(0,5);
}

You started with the process we recommend, so it's great
you've already figured out it's not a bug in the model.

The Stan code's very tight, but I can make a couple
suggestions.

First, move the declaration and definition of
Sigma_beta to the generated_quantities block because you
don't use them in the model. This will be a big savings
if the matrix is large.

Second, the expression

exp(-exp(lrc[jj[n]])

is just an underflow waiting to happen. It'll basically underflow
if lrc > 6.5 or so. Is there a way to express this not on
the exp(-exp()) scale?

It's odd that there'd be a stack overflow. That indicates
recursion going beyond the max depth that C++ can handle. We
wrote everything in Stan iteratively to avoid this issue.

We can run in CmdStan to see if it's an R or Stan issue. Daniel
and I are both on the road now, so I don't have anywhere I can
try a long-running model.

- Bob

Thanks Bob. Very helpful. I moved Sigma_beta to the generated quantities but it only improved speed on a smaller data (1K individuals, 6K observations) set by about 3%. This isn't too surprising I think since that's only a 3x3 matrix. But still very useful for me to note for future work.

As for exp(- exp(lrc) * time) and underflow issues, I'd prefer to keep lrc (log rate of change) to be sampled on a log scale since, as a rate, that is the more meaningful scale to sample it from a normal distribution (it's multinormally distributed with the other parameters). I plotted the model for lrc =seq(-3, 3, len=9) on both scales to double check that the spacing is indeed problematic on the un-logged scale. As you can see from the attached figure, indeed it is.

But in thinking about this I realized that I have ridiculous priors right now and I wonder if that's part of the problem. I kept
to_vector(gamma) ~ Normal(0,5)
from the manual code. But the first row of my gamma matrix are intercepts for each of the non-linear model parameters. And I know a priori that R0 should be in the range of of 2-6 and Asym should be 5-7. lrc is probably in the range of -2 to 2. So I changed the priors to:
  gamma[1,1] ~ normal(6, 5);
  gamma[1,2] ~ normal(4, 5);
  gamma[1,3] ~ normal(0, 2);
  gamma[2] ~ normal(0,5);
This did not speed up the HMC iterations at all on the smaller test set (1K indiv). But I'm hoping that by narrowing the prior on lrc to normal(0,2) it would reduce the chance of underflow, though I'm not sure if I'm thinking about this clearly.

I'll rerun it on a full-sized (ie size of the eventual real data) data set tonight & report what happens in the morning.

They can be a big problem, especially in problems with
overdispersion (which includes a lot of latent-parameter
models and the negative binomial).

> I kept
> to_vector(gamma) ~ Normal(0,5)

> from the manual code. But the first row of my gamma matrix are intercepts for each of the non-linear model parameters. And I know a priori that R0 should be in the range of of 2-6 and R0 and Asym should be 5-7. lrc is probably in the range of -2 to 2. So I changed the priors to:

What it'll do is keep things closer to 0.

Also, running something more constrained than those Cauchy
priors can help, too --- they allow big outliers. So you might
want to see in the traceplots or with max or something whether
some parameters are going to extreme values.

parts:
Well, those clearly haven't converged. Are the chains close
and just not mixing, or are they clearly stuck in different
modes? That is, does it look like running longer might help?

I don't know if you're getting any divergences here (typically
indicated by warmup messages, but you can also pull them out
of the fit in RStan and they're printed in CmdStan), but if you
are, you probably want to start with a smaller step size and
up the adapt_delta target above its default of 0.8 (perhaps as
high as 0.99). That'll keep step size down and allow the gradients
to do a better job of mimicking the curvature. But it'll slow
down the iterations (at the benefit of getting higher n_eff per
iteration).

The problem with increasing data is that it can increase posterior
curvature along narrow ridges, making it harder for the Hamiltonian
simulation to find a large step size to make large moves. Sometimes
this is good and you actually get sublinear growth with data. Sometimes
it's bad and constrains the parameters and makes them correlated in
a way that makes it much harder to move in Euclidean space with just
a gradient. So you'll probably see the number of leapfrog steps going up and
the step size going down as you get more data to try to compensate.

- Bob

are, you probably want to start with a smaller step size and
up the adapt_delta target above its default of 0.8 (perhaps as
high as 0.99).  That'll keep step size down and allow the gradients
to do a better job of mimicking the curvature.  But it'll slow
down the iterations (at the benefit of getting higher n_eff per
iteration).

The problem with increasing data is that it can increase posterior
curvature along narrow ridges, making it harder for the Hamiltonian
simulation to find a large step size to make large moves.  Sometimes
this is good and you actually get sublinear growth with data.  Sometimes
it's bad and constrains the parameters and makes them correlated in
a way that makes it much harder to move in Euclidean space with just
a gradient.  So you'll probably see the number of leapfrog steps going up and
the step size going down as you get more data to try to compensate.

I've also seen this lead to non-convergence when some chains find the narrow ridges and others never do (and explore a much broader parameter space).  You can ususally tell that from trace plots or just looking at means/variances for multiple chains.

Krzysztof

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] optimizing hierarchical non-linear regression
parts:
Bob: I've attached trace plots for both the 10K & 70K models. It looks to me like some parameters have the chains coming close but not mixing (gamma, sigma), but others (the correlation/covariance matrix CovsPatsOmega/Sigma_beta) are not coming close in the amount of time the chain runs. So it does seem like there is a thin likelihood ridge for the fixed effects (gamma) but not necessarily for their correlations. I'm not sure what this means practically. The problem is clearly worse for the 70K model.

Michael: based on your advice I've implemented a centered version of the code below.  I went through the 2013 paper but must admit that I still don't quite follow the rationale for non-centering for small data sets and centering for large data sets. It is unclear how much better/worse the centered version does on small-intermediate size data sets thus far. Some parameters have greater n_eff, some have smaller. I suspect it's hard to tell from only 2 chains. I'm in the process of getting this workflow setup on HPC and will then run batch fits with & without centering, & for a range of deltas (.8,.9,.95,.99) with 24 chains each run, and will then report the results.

My centered model is:

data {
  int<lower=0> Nobs; // # observations
  int<lower=1> Npat; // # individuals
int<lower=1> NcovsPat; // # individuals-level predictors (1, sex)
int<lower=1> NasymParm; // # parameters for non-linear model
int<lower=1,upper=Npat> jj[Nobs]; // individuals for observation
vector[Nobs] time;    // time of follow up
matrix[Npat,NcovsPat] Upat;    // individuals-level predictors [1, sex]_jj

vector[Nobs] y;    // outcome
}
parameters {
corr_matrix[NasymParm] Omega; // correlation matrix for predictor-coefficients
vector<lower=0>[NasymParm] tau; // prior scale on covar-var matrix

matrix[NcovsPat,NasymParm] gamma; // individuals-level coefficients (1,sex)X(Asym,R0,lrc)
  vector[NasymParm] beta[Npat];    // each individual's asymptotic parameters

real<lower=0> sigma; // obs-level error
}

model {
  matrix[NasymParm,NasymParm] Sigma_beta; // covar-var matrix
  vector[Nobs] Mod_jj;
  vector[NasymParm] u_gamma_t[Npat];
  Sigma_beta <- quad_form_diag(Omega,tau);
  tau ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
  Omega ~ lkj_corr(2);

gamma[1,1] ~ normal(6, 5);
  gamma[1,2] ~ normal(4, 5);
  gamma[1,3] ~ normal(0, 2);
  gamma[2] ~ normal(0,5);

for(j in 1:Npat)
    u_gamma_t[j] <- (Upat[j] * gamma)';
  beta ~ multi_normal(u_gamma_t, Sigma_beta);
for (n in 1:Nobs) {

Mod_jj[n] <- beta[jj[n],1] + (beta[jj[n],2] - beta[jj[n],1]) * exp(-exp(beta[jj[n],3]) * time[n]);
  }
  y ~ normal(Mod_jj, sigma);
}

It depends on the data and how it's drawn. What looks
like an "outlier" in a small data set might become a well-delineated
mode in a bigger data set. Especially if one mode's much
higher mass than the other.

> I’ll definitely run longer. As for (a) and (b), my impression was that increasing delta (the target acceptance rate) automatically reduces the step size (which is adaptively tuned by NUTS), and that therefore I can do both (a) and (b) just by tuning this parameter. Or were you suggesting to explicitly set the step size through some other way, like switching to an HMC algorithm?

Not quite. There is an initial step size (a), which then gets
adapted based on the target acceptance rate (b). Changing the
target acceptance rate has no effect on the initial step size.
Usually if you need a higher acceptance rate, you want to start
with a smaller step size so you don't run too far into the tail
during warmup by taking too-big steps. It'll mainly cut down on
warnings and make convergence smoother and less variable across
chains than anything else.

parts: The standard initial stepsize is 1.0. What I usually do is manually tweak to a point where I no longer get divergent iterations during sampling. You don't want to go low than necessary as it will make your sampling unnecessarily inefficient (NUTS treedepth goes up when stepsize is lower).
